html:
Diné Bikéyah, "the people's land", is the Navajo homeland in the American Southwest, bounded in tradition by four sacred mountains: Blanca Peak, Mount Taylor, the San Francisco Peaks and Hesperus Mountain. The Diné speak an Athabaskan language, related to Apache and to languages of north-west Canada. Their ancestors came south from there, probably between 1300 and 1500.

In the Southwest they learned farming and weaving from the Pueblo peoples, and took up sheep and horses from the Spanish. Herding made them rich, and Navajo blankets and later rugs and silver became famous.

Raids and counter raids with Spanish, Mexican and American settlers ended in 1863 and 1864, when US troops burned their fields and forced thousands of Diné on the Long Walk to Bosque Redondo in New Mexico. A treaty of 1868 let them return to part of their land. That reservation grew into the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation in the United States. In the Second World War Navajo code talkers sent Marine messages in their own language. Earlier maps show them as Navajo.
